D018-D013_h001.question:
I’ve been struggling for about a year now—ever since that incident at City Hall when the explosion went off during the council meeting. I was nearby, helping with documents. I can still feel the blast, the heat—it comes back like I’m there, sometimes while I’m sitting at my desk or even driving home. I’ll snap out of it and realize I’ve been gripping the wheel, heart slamming, shaking for minutes afterward. I can’t seem to calm down after things like that.

I don’t enjoy much anymore—used to love playing guitar on weekends, but now it just feels pointless. My wife notices, but I can’t explain how empty it all feels. I keep thinking about who allowed that man into the building. There were warnings—I believe someone higher up ignored them. That fuels a lot of my anger. I wake up with that same horror I felt that day, like it’s stuck in my chest. Choosing what to wear, what to eat—simple things—drag on forever because I can’t decide. It’s like my mind freezes. The sadness is there, yes, but it’s tied to *that day*. It doesn’t feel like depression—it feels like I’m still living in the aftermath.

A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h002.question:
I’ve been messed up since the accident last spring—when my roommate and I got into that bad car crash. I was driving. He didn’t make it. Sometimes, out of nowhere, I’m right back there—smell the burnt rubber, hear the metal crunch, feel the wheel lock. I’ll drop whatever I’m holding, like I’m back in the driver’s seat, frozen. It’s happened in class, in the dining hall… it’s humiliating.

I can’t stand being around people now. Everyone says “it wasn’t your fault,” but I should’ve slowed down, I should’ve taken a different route. I barely text my friends, skip group meetings, even avoid the campus shuttle. I feel tense all the time—jump at every bus horn or slamming door. My focus is shot. I stare at a textbook page for 20 minutes and don’t remember a word.  

I’ve been down, yeah—empty, tired, don’t care about school—but it’s not just sadness. It’s like the crash never ended. It’s always with me. The fear, the guilt, the flashbacks—they’re all tied to that moment. I don’t think I’ll ever be safe from it.
D018-D013_h002.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Major Depressive Disorder
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h003.question:

D018-D013_h004.question:

If someone walks into the room suddenly, even at work, I jump so badly I drop things—just yesterday I spilled coffee because my colleague came up behind me. I startle at quick movements, like shadows shifting. It’s like my body won’t relax.  

I keep having these waves of nausea or tightness in my chest when I pass the neighborhood where it happened, even if I’m not fully thinking about it. I don’t want to go near that part of the city anymore.  

I feel… broken. Ashamed, like I should’ve handled it differently. I blame the public defender office leadership—they pushed me to go alone despite the risks. Why didn’t they protect me?

D018-D013_h005.question:

I found him in the hallway. I don’t remember much—just his face, the cold metal, how everyone froze. Since then, I can’t stop seeing it. Just last week, a teacher patted my shoulder from behind, and I jumped so hard I dropped my keys—my heart raced like I was back there.  

I avoid the east wing where it happened. I cancel staff meetings if they’re scheduled there. My husband says I’ve changed—don’t talk much, don’t want to go out. I didn’t even go to our daughter’s recital. It’s not that I’m sad, exactly—it’s more like rage keeps bubbling up. I blame the school board for not funding security, even the boy’s parents—I know it’s not fair, but I can’t shut it off.  

Some days, my head feels foggy, like I’m walking through water. And I’m just… angry all the time. The sadness? It’s there, sure—but only since everything after that day became unbearable. It’s not life that feels pointless. It’s that moment—that one moment—that ruined everything.
D018-D013_h005.options:

    B. Major Depressive Disorder

    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation)

D018-D013_h006.question:

I avoid thinking about it. I won’t pass that clinic, won’t go on evening visits anymore. I’ve stopped talking to my coworkers about certain things. And I can’t explain it, but I don’t feel the same way toward my husband. I know I love him, but the warmth—the affection—just doesn’t come.  

I’ve been sad, yeah. Tired. But it’s not just depression. It’s like I’m haunted. The flashbacks, the gaps in memory, the way I react—it all started *because* of what happened. It’s not just sadness—it’s like I’m still living it.

I’ve been driving a taxi for over twenty years, and I used to handle the night shifts no problem. But ever since that night last March—when I picked up a passenger who pulled a knife, robbed me, and threatened to kill me—I haven’t been the same. I keep seeing it again and again, like a movie stuck in my head. Out of nowhere, I’ll feel his hand on my shoulder, hear his voice. It happens at red lights, in traffic, even when I’m off the job.

Since then, I just feel… empty. I can’t connect with my kids like I used to. My ex asked if I’d come to their birthday, but being around them felt phony—I couldn’t fake warmth I don’t feel. I feel ashamed, like I should’ve fought back, done something. That shame eats at me.

I’ve also been snapping—at passengers, my sister, strangers. Last week I cursed out a man for being five seconds late getting in the car. I know it’s not right, but I can’t help it. I’m tired all the time, sleeping maybe three hours a night, and I don’t care about much. But honestly, these feelings—this numbness, the anger, the guilt—they all trace back to that night. It’s like I haven’t left that backseat.

I’ve been having these awful dreams lately—night after night, I’m back at the scene of that car accident from two years ago. I see my husband, the twisted metal, the flashing lights… it feels so real. I wake up sweating and can’t fall back asleep. Since he passed, I just feel on edge all the time. I jump at the smallest noises—the mail slot clinking, the furnace turning on. I’m always braced for something terrible to happen, even though I know logically I’m safe here in my home.

I used to enjoy knitting for the grandkids, going to church potlucks, even gardening. Now nothing gives me joy. When one of my sons told me how proud he was of my afghans, I just stared at them. I didn’t feel anything. I want to feel happy, but it’s like that part of me shut down. And sometimes, I get furious—out of nowhere. Last week, I screamed at my daughter because she rearranged the silverware drawer. I didn’t mean to, but the anger just exploded.

It’s not just sadness—it’s like my whole life is haunted by that moment in the ambulance when I realized he was gone. That accident changed everything. The dreams, the fear, the anger—it’s all tied to it. I’ve felt this way most days for over a year now.
